header.text: <instructions>Read the following text from a folktale. This excerpt is about Aladdin.</instructions>

contents.text: His son, who was called Aladdin, had been brought up in a very careless and idle manner, and by that means had contracted many vicious habits. He was stubborn and disobedient to his father and mother, who, when he grew up, could not keep him indoors.

The mother, finding that her son would not follow his father's business, shut up the shop and sold off the implements of trade. With the money she received for them, and what she could get by spinning cotton, she thought to support herself and her son.
Aladdin, who cared so little for his mother that whenever she scolded him he would berate her, gave himself entirely over to his idle habits.
Adapted from Unknown, The Arabian Nights

contents.text: He excitedly pulled more figs and dates out of his pockets and put them in a chipped bowl. And then, from the sash that held up his pants, he pulled fresh almonds and smoked pistachios…and from somewhere under his scrap of a shirt, cashews.

header.text: <instructions>Read the following text from a memoir. This excerpt is about Anne Morrow Lindbergh's 1931 flight to China.</instructions>

contents.text: As I walked out of the building two women ran up to me.
"Oh, Mrs. Lindbergh," said one, "the women of America are so anxious to know about your clothes."
"And I," said the other, "want to write a little article about your housekeeping in the ship. Where do you put the lunch boxes?"

I felt depressed, as I generally do when women reporters ask me conventionally feminine questions. I feel as they must feel when they are given those questions to ask. I feel slightly insulted. Over in the corner my husband is being asked vital masculine questions, clean-cut steely technicalities or broad abstractions. But I am asked about clothes and lunch boxes.
From Anne Morrow Lindbergh, North to the Orient. Copyright 1935 by Anne Morrow Lindbergh

choices.text: Lindbergh was disappointed in the questions reporters asked her.

contents.text: Surrounded by reporters, photographers, and Movietone men with their whirring cameras, we waited as two mechanics made a final check of the Sirius. contents.text: Now the queen's niece, who was next in line for the throne…was arriving in person to ask Congress to restore her nation to her people. The assembled crowd chattered in anticipation. What would she look like? What would she wear? How would she behave?

header.text: <instructions>Read the following text from a historical novel. This excerpt is about Hawaiian princess Kaʻiulani's 1893 visit to New York City.</instructions>

contents.text: The pier ahead of us was crowded with reporters and ordinary citizens who had come to see me arrive. I do not believe they were there out of admiration, but rather to satisfy their curiosity. I found the size of the crowd daunting, but buried this thought deep inside, so that I would not be distracted from the task at hand. I may no longer officially be a princess, but I certainly behave as one.
Once we had disembarked, the crowd moved to surround me. There were so many strangers pressing close, and shouting questions, that it took all of my strength to keep my expression immobile and calm.

header.text: <instructions>Read the following text from a myth. This excerpt is about warriors' afterlife in Valhalla.</instructions>

contents.text: To arrive in Valhalla, the fallen warriors had to cross a large, noisy river. Once there, Odin welcomed them heartily. He had straw strewn on the benches in the hall to make them comfortable; he had all the goblets polished.…

And what a fine routine met these warriors there in Valhalla. Every night they feasted on overflowing platters of pork from the beast Saehrimnir, roasted in the cauldron Eldhrimnir by the soot-covered cook Andhrimnir.… Every day they battled together, and those who fell in these heavenly battles simply rose again at the end of the day and marched through the 540 doors of the hall to join the feast anew, since everything regenerated of its own accord.
From Donna Jo Napoli, Treasury of Norse Mythology: Stories of Intrigue, Trickery, Love, and Revenge. Copyright 2015 by Donna Jo Napoli

contents.text: In the fields surrounding Valhalla, the reaped warriors who had chosen to remain in Asgard did what they were always doing. Fighting. Thor, son of Odin and greatest warrior of them all, was among them, taking on hundreds at a time. Some called this training; Thor just called it fun.

header.text: <instructions>Read the following text from a memoir. This excerpt is about the early days of the Jamestown colony.</instructions>

contents.text: Within ten days, barely ten of us could either go or even stand, such extreme weakness and sickness oppressed us. And none will marvel at that, if they consider the cause and reason, which was this: while the ships stayed, our food allowance was somewhat improved by a daily portion of biscuit, which the sailors would steal to sell, give, or exchange with us. But when they departed, there remained no place of relief but the shared rations. And that was half a pint of wheat, and as much barley, boiled with water for a man a day. And this, having fried some twenty-six weeks in the ship's hold, contained as many worms as grains.
From Captain John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia, New-England, and the Summer Isles

table.text: Studies have shown that some crows recognize human faces. In one experiment, a group of researchers wore different rubber masks, some of them more dangerous-looking than others. Then, the researchers in the more dangerous-looking masks temporarily trapped a group of American crows. After the birds were released, the group of masked researchers returned. The previously trapped crows sounded an immediate alarm and then dive-bombed the researchers—but not all of them. They sought revenge only on those they recognized in the dangerous-looking masks.

Scientists are learning that certain species of crows are highly intelligent. As one of the few non-primates that use tools, crows have been observed using sticks as spears or hooks and even bending wire to make new tools. Scientists have also found that crows can form bonds with humans. There are reports of crows bringing "thank you" gifts to people who have fed them. The odd assortment of gifts might include a button or a screw, or even small bones.

content.text: Which sentence best combines the main, or central, ideas of both texts?

When crows recognize humans, they often deliver objects as gifts to say thank you for food left out for them.

table.text: Astronauts living and working on the International Space Station must adapt everyday routines to the conditions around them, including personal hygiene. Without flowing water, astronauts use a washcloth and a no-rinse solution to take a shower or wash their hands. Astronauts can brush their teeth with normal toothbrushes, but many use an edible toothpaste so they do not have to rinse. Even cutting hair is different in space: astronauts use a vacuum attachment to prevent clipped hairs from flying around the space station.

Living in the weightless environment of space can degrade astronauts' bodies. On Earth, human muscles and bones stay strong due in part to the everyday work of overcoming the forces of gravity. On the International Space Station, because astronauts are weightless and float around, they do not use their bodies in the same way. Therefore, their muscles can weaken, and their bones can start to thin. To combat these effects, astronauts take dietary supplements and exercise for two hours every day.
